title: Why ask for a small yes first?
principle: A small yes first makes the big yes easier.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a test from 1966 in California. Researchers asked people who owned homes to put a big, ugly sign on their front lawn. It said "Drive Carefully". Most said no, but one group said yes much more often.

screens.title: The small ask
screens.text: Two weeks earlier, someone had asked that group to put a small "Be a safe driver" sign in a window or car. That was easy to agree to. Two weeks later, a different person asked them to put up the big lawn sign.

screens.prompt: Of those asked only about the big sign, 17 in 100 said yes. How many said yes if first asked about the small sign?
screens.why: About 76 in 100. Being asked something small two weeks earlier, by a different person, made people more than four times as likely to agree to the big one.

screens.title: Commitment and consistency
screens.text: This is called commitment and consistency, or "foot in the door". People like to keep doing what they've agreed to do. Saying no later can feel wrong to them. So agreeing to something small makes it easier to agree to something big.

screens.title: It's used on you
screens.text: You see this often: "just answer three quick questions", a ₹1 first month followed by full price, or a free account before a paid plan. Each small yes makes the next easier. Later studies found the effect was real, but smaller than 76 against 17.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: A lawn sign and a cake order work the same way. It's mid-October. An IT office in the tech park has 120 staff and about 10 birthdays a month. You meet its manager for a short, free chat. She won't sign a year's plan with a baker she's never tried.

screens.prompt: During the chat, you offer one ₹850 cake for Friday's birthday. The manager says, "Let me think." What do you say?

options.label: "Can we talk again on Monday at 11?"
"This price lasts only until this week"

screens.why: Yes. Agreeing to talk again on a fixed date is a small yes. People often keep promises they've made, so the Monday meeting at 11 is more likely to happen.

wrong.a: That's polite, but you haven't agreed on anything. Busy managers may forget. Ask for one small next step with a date: "Monday at 11?"
wrong.c: A false deadline puts pressure on her. People who feel pushed may say no. Instead, agree on one small next step and a date.

screens.prompt: Here are five steps to get the office's yearly plan. They are in the wrong order. Put the first step at the top.
steps: Offer one ₹850 cake for this Friday's birthday
On Monday, ask what the manager's staff liked about it
Agree to a one-month trial and a date to talk again
Meet on that date and review the month together
Offer the next step: a longer plan
screens.why: Good. Each step is small and useful on its own. The manager tells you what her staff liked, using her own words. Then she chooses the next step. Each yes makes the next one easier.

screens.prompt: You want more offices to try your cakes. Which small first step is fair to ask for?

options.label: A ₹1 trial that becomes ₹10,000 next month without telling them
A free cake for signing a year's plan now
A ₹300 cupcake box for one office meeting

screens.why: Yes. The cupcake box is useful even if the office buys nothing else. The office can then decide if it wants more. A fair small step must leave the buyer free to say no.

wrong.a: A ₹1 trial that becomes ₹10,000 without making it clear is unfair. The small step must be useful on its own, and the buyer must choose whether to take the big step.
wrong.b: You're asking for a big yes first and offering a gift to get it. The small step should come before the big one, not at the same time.

screens.setup: It's the end of November. The one-month trial went well: 10 cakes, and everyone liked them. You meet on the agreed date. The manager feels that signing for a whole year at ₹850 a cake is too much right now. Each cake leaves you ₹450.
screens.question: What do you say?

options.label: "You've come this far. Don't waste the trial"
options.outcome: The manager feels pushed and guilty. She decides to ask other bakers too. In December, the office orders nothing from you. You earn ₹0 from it.
options.why: You used the trial to make her feel guilty about saying no. That's like the sunk-cost mistake from Unit 1. People may refuse when they feel forced.
options.better: Offer a three-month plan and agree on a date to talk again.

options.label: "Let's try three months, then talk again"
options.outcome: She agrees to three months: about 30 cakes, leaving you ₹13,500. In February, she agrees to a year at ₹850: 120 cakes, leaving you ₹54,000.
options.why: You offered a smaller next step instead of asking for the whole year. Each yes made the next one easier.

options.label: "I'll charge ₹750 per cake for the year"
options.outcome: She agrees to the year immediately. 120 cakes now leave you ₹350 each: ₹42,000. That's ₹12,000 less than at ₹850.
options.why: You got the year's plan, but earned less on every cake. A smaller next step could have helped you keep the ₹850 price.
options.better: Offer a three-month plan and agree on a date to talk again.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: The line again: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. A small step must be useful on its own. Let the buyer choose the big step. Don't make someone feel guilty for saying no after they've started.
Ask for a small ___ first, because people like to stay true to what they've ___.
screens.why: Yes. The small window sign led to the big lawn sign. One Friday cake led to a one-month trial, then three months, then a year.

summary: Commitment and consistency: once we agree to something, agreeing again feels easier.
After "let me think", agree on one small next step and a date.
The small step must be useful on its own. Never make buyers feel guilty about what they've already started.

cards.front: A gym wants new members. What should it offer first?
cards.back: A small yes first makes the big yes easier.

cards.front: A buyer says "let me think". What do you say?
cards.back: Agree on one small next step and a date. People often keep promises they've made.

cards.front: A trial buyer isn't ready for the big plan. What should you avoid saying?
cards.back: Making buyers feel guilty about what they've started is unfair. Offer a smaller next step instead.

sources.label: Freedman and Fraser, Compliance without pressure: the foot-in-the-door technique (1966)
